item.content:
Formatting of this note is different from the original.
Influenza, Seasonal
You have been seen for influenza. This is sometimes called “the flu.” Often, no tests are done but influenza is strongly suspected. For this reason, many doctors are giving the diagnosis of “Influenza-Like Illness.”
Influenza is very contagious. This means it spreads easily among people. It is caused by the influenza virus. That is why it is also called "the flu." It affects the respiratory tract. This includes the nose, throat and lungs. In some people, it can cause very serious problems. This usually happens with the very young and the elderly. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that an average of 5-20% of people living in the U.S. are affected by regular seasonal influenza every year. This includes influenza A and B. More than 200,000 people are hospitalized from flu complications. About 36,000 people die from flu-related causes every year.
STAY AWAY FROM OTHER PEOPLE WHO ARE NOT YET AFFECTED. THIS IS THE BEST WAY TO STOP THE SPREAD OF INFLUENZA. YOU CAN SPREAD THE FLU FROM ONE DAY BEFORE YOU GET SICK UP TO 7 DAYS AFTER YOU DEVELOP SYMPTOMS.
UNTIL IT IS CONFIRMED THAT YOU DON’T HAVE INFLUENZA, YOU SHOULD:
· Stay off from work. You should be off of work for 7 days from the start of symptoms or until the viral cultures show you don’t have influenza.
· Stay home and do not go into public places.
· Stay away from others in the house.
· Wash your hands often.
· Cover your mouth when you sneeze or cough. Use your sleeve to cover your mouth and nose. Do not use your hand.
People you live with and those you had close contact with, should watch for flu signs. People with a serious medical condition or who are pregnant should tell their doctor they were exposed to flu.
Influenza often happens as an epidemic in the fall and winter. This means many people get the flu virus at the same time. It spreads from person to person. Over the centuries, there have been epidemics of many different “new” strains of influenza.
Most people with influenza get these symptoms:
· High fevers: Fevers are often higher than 102°F or 39°C.
· Cough. A dry, hacking cough is most common.
· Headache: The headache may be worse with the fever. It can be there even when the temperature is normal.
· Muscle aches. Many people have muscle pain. These are called “myalgias.”
· Sore throat.
You may also feel weak and fatigued (tired). You may also get a runny nose or congestion (stuffy nose). Some people will have mild stomach symptoms. This can include vomiting (throwing up). Sometimes it includes mild diarrhea.
Influenza does not primarily involve vomiting and diarrhea. Vomiting and diarrhea are usually symptoms of a completely different problem. This problem is called "gastroenteritis." Gastroenteritis is often called "the stomach flu." This is how the confusion came about! True influenza is a lung infection.
During flu season, influenza can sometimes be diagnosed without tests. This can be done if a patient has the right set of symptoms. These are called "classic flu" symptoms. Sometimes flu testing is done. This is usually with a test called a “Rapid Influenza Test.” Results show up in a few minutes. The test is not perfect. It misses many cases. Sometimes, more specialized tests are done. These tests pick up more of the cases. However, results are not ready for a few days.
Usually, the "flu shot" is good at preventing influenza. Some years the shot is less effective than others. You can sometimes still get severe influenza, even if you had the immunization (shot). You can still get "the stomach flu," (not true influenza), even after the flu shot. Today, the current Influenza vaccine is designed to protect against seasonal Influenza A and B and H1N1. There are good supplies of the vaccine available. It is being given to all persons who would like to receive it.
Influenza treatment depends on how early in the course of the illness you are when diagnosed. With medicine, you may feel better sooner. Medicines do not cure the flu. However, they do help your body fight the infection.
Some antiviral medicines may help symptoms. They often only help if they are started in the first few days of the illness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) makes recommendations as to who should get the antiviral medicine. Your doctor will decide if the medicine may be helpful for you.
Most patients get better with simple things like rest, fluids and a little time. Acetaminophen (Tylenol®) and/or ibuprofen (Advil® or Motrin®) can also help. Older patients or those with serious medical problems may have worse problems with the flu. They may need additional care.
Treatment of influenza usually is at home. Some patients need to be in the hospital. These are often very young and very old patients and those with severe symptoms. It also includes those with other serious medical problems.
It is OK for you to go home now. Follow the instructions above about staying away from others!
YOU SHOULD SEEK MEDICAL ATTENTION IMMEDIATELY, EITHER HERE OR AT THE NEAREST EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT, IF ANY OF THE FOLLOWING OCCURS:
· You have shortness of breath, wheezing or any severe problems breathing.
· You have a headache that gets worse or a stiff neck.
· You feel lightheaded or faint.
· You have chest pain.
· You have a cough and fever (temperature higher than 100.4ºF or 38ºC) that seem to come back AFTER your flu symptoms get better. This can be a different kind of lung infection called “pneumonia,” that sometimes happens after the flu.
· You feel sicker at any time or do not get better as expected. You can expect to feel sick for a week or so.
· You have any other new symptoms or concerns.
If you can't follow up with your doctor, or if at any time you feel you need to be rechecked or seen again, come back here or go to the nearest emergency department.
Tylenol and Advil as needed for fevers.
You are outside the window for treatment with Tamiflu.
Drink plenty of fluids
